gao-gaoreports-gao-05-280r:
Defense Base Act Insurance, GAO-05-280R of April 29, 2005, is a letter that opens a review of injury cover for Iraq rebuild crews. Since March 2003, U.S. agencies have hired firms to rebuild Iraq amid ongoing strife. A law called the Defense Base Act gives their staff medical and disability aid if hurt, and death aid to kin if killed. The taxpayer pays the cover cost through deal prices.

Over 100 members of Congress asked GAO to probe Iraq costs, this one among them. GAO sets out to price the cover bought under the act. It sets out to grade how the act is run. A full review is needed, the title holds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-310r:
DOD and VA Health Care, GAO-05-310R of February 28, 2005, tracks a joint fund meant to make two health giants share. The Defense and Veterans Affairs systems serve about 16.8 million people. Their care cost an estimated $58 billion for fiscal year 2005, split $30.4 billion and $27.7 billion. A 1982 law let them buy, sell, and swap care. A 2003 law added prize cash for joint plans.

Each side must put at least $15 million a year into the fund, for fiscal years 2004 through 2007. Local sites pitch joint plans and vie for the cash. GAO grades the rules, the tests for picks, and the first steps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-470r:
Rules for closing military grocery stores are examined in a GAO letter, GAO-05-470R, sent on April 26, 2005. The Defense Commissary Agency runs 273 commissaries selling groceries to service members and families at low prices. Yearly reviews weigh quality of life against business results for each store. Congress asked whether a 2003 push to close 14 stores gave quality of life its due.

New guidance issued in March 2005 made quality of life a primary factor in future reviews, though none had yet run under it. The 14 stores had been picked in 2003 mainly for weak finances or few active-duty shoppers. That choice seemed at odds with policy that both factors be weighed together. After protests from the services and Congress, the department kept all 14 stores open. Six had improved their finances, and eight were kept for quality of life and other reasons.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-500r:
The Catholic War Veterans of the United States of America is the subject of GAO letter GAO-05-500R, issued on June 10, 2005. The letter deals with the audit report for the group's fiscal year ended June 30, 2003. The corporation works to keep the nation focused on the needs of veterans. It also speaks for their widows and orphans and defends the Constitution.

Under title 36 of the U.S. Code, such chartered bodies must file detailed yearly financial statements. An outside public accountant must audit them. The House Judiciary Committee asked GAO to read this audit report for any breach of those duties. GAO read the statements and notes and made limited checks of the numbers. It reported no breach worth flagging. The outside auditor found the statements fairly presented under generally accepted accounting principles. GAO did not examine the auditor's own work papers and offered no audit opinion.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-510r:
GAO letter GAO-05-510R (June 10, 2005) reports GAO's read of audit reports for the Military Chaplains Association of the United States of America. The association helps chaplains do their work well. It works to strengthen the military chaplaincy and to draw new people into it. The fiscal years covered ended December 31, 2003, and December 31, 2002.

Charter law requires yearly statements that show assets and liabilities and give reasonable detail on income and expenses. An outside accountant must audit them. GAO read the statements, notes, and audit reports, and checked the data with analytical procedures. It also spoke briefly with the auditor about possible gains in reporting quality. No failure to comply with the law was identified. The auditors found the statements fairly presented under U.S. generally accepted accounting principles.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-570r:
Why military satellite programs keep running over cost and time is probed in a GAO letter, GAO-05-570R, dated June 23, 2005. The Defense Department planned to spend more than $23 billion in fiscal year 2006 on satellites and related space systems. Satellites warn of missile attack, guide forces, and carry military traffic. Their programs have a long record of growth in cost and delay. GAO gathered voices from across the field to find the drivers.

Officials and managers pointed to a missing overall investment strategy. The department starts more programs than it can afford, the letter reports. It rarely ranks them for funding. Start dates get set before a sound business case exists for the program. Those pressures then echo through design, contracting, and oversight. GAO based the letter on a decade of its own satellite reviews and on past department studies.  The letter names the incentives that reform must change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-580r:
Who made the key calls in studies behind the 2004 overtime rule is the question in a GAO letter, GAO-05-580R, dated June 3, 2005. The Labor Department updated the rule that decides who earns time-and-a-half pay past 40 hours a week. It hired the CONSAD Research Corporation to help gauge the rule's impact. Congress wanted the firm's duties and its actual work pinned down. GAO read both contracts and traced the tasks.

The contracts gave the firm a support role: cost and benefit reports, and studies of effects on business and on state and local government.  The department still asked the firm to count workers who might gain or lose overtime pay. The second contract named that worker study outright. It also required detail on workers' ages, schooling, and jobs.  GAO found the firm gave technical and analytic help, while the department made every key decision.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-590r:
GAO-05-590R, dated June 23, 2005, carries GAO's remarks on a representation letter from the Farm Credit System Insurance Corporation. The letter under review is the older one in this set: it covers fiscal year 2003, not 2004. The corporation insures the farm credit system's debt. Its written confirmations feed the audit of the federal government's combined statements. GAO found faults in two of five key areas.

Like most agencies in this round, the corporation sent no materiality thresholds with its letter. Its letter also included just 20 of the 25 standard representations that applied. One more was partial, and 4 were left out entirely. GAO made two recommendations to the chief financial officer, aimed at those gaps. It further recommended that the chairman of the audit committee take part. He would work with the outside audit firm and the corporation to make future letters complete. The report treats the flaws as simple to fix.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-600r:
The Department of Homeland Security's representation letter for fiscal year 2004 is covered in GAO report GAO-05-600R, issued on July 14, 2005. The young department's letter feeds the audit of the government's combined financial statements. GAO reviewed it in the same five key areas used across this series. Two areas needed improvement, and both were about missing support rather than wrong figures.

The department gave no materiality thresholds with its letter. Those thresholds show which matters it treated as big enough to count, and the Treasury needs them for the government-wide letter. The summary of uncorrected misstatements was incomplete too. It did not split errors in accounts with other agencies from errors in accounts with the public. GAO made two recommendations to the chief financial officer. It also asked the acting inspector general, with the outside audit firm, to help ensure that later letters meet the standard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-610r:
Two of five key areas needed work in the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation's fiscal year 2004 letter, GAO report GAO-05-610R of July 22, 2005. The letter carried 31 of the 32 standard representations that applied, but one was only partly stated. The corporation also gave no summary sorting unadjusted errors between government accounts and public accounts.

GAO made two targeted recommendations to the finance chief. It asked the Inspector General, with the outside audit firm, to help meet both points. The finance chief and the assistant inspector general for audits agreed and pledged fixes for the next year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-680r:
Master plans for overseas bases are reviewed in GAO letter GAO-05-680R of June 27, 2005. Congress ordered full plans for each regional command so building money is not wasted on bases about to close. The Pentagon's guidance asked for more than Congress required, which GAO backs. One gap remains: the guidance omits residual value, the worth of sites handed back to host nations, often cut by cleanup costs.

Commands mostly followed the rules but varied in detail. Without the missing figures, GAO warns, Congress cannot see what returned land means for future U.S. building bills. Yearly updates run through 2009.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-770r:
Written answers on the Defense Department's new personnel system make up GAO-05-770R, a letter dated May 31, 2005. GAO had testified to the Senate Armed Services panel on April 14, 2005. Senators sent follow-up questions after that hearing. This letter answers them for the record.

The answers take up the design and rollout of the National Security Personnel System. That system resets pay, hiring, and discipline rules for defense civilian staff. The letter lets readers see GAO's stance on the main doubts raised at the hearing. It sits beside GAO's wider body of work urging care, staff input, and clear measures in the change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-780r:
The yearly check on a threat reduction program is GAO-05-780R, a letter dated July 1, 2005. The Defense Department runs the Cooperative Threat Reduction program. By law, it sends Congress a report each year with a five-year plan. GAO must assess that plan within 90 days. The department sent its fiscal year 2006 report on February 23, 2005.

GAO briefed congressional staff on May 23, 2005. The letter records the scope of that check. GAO tested whether the five-year plan meets what the law asks. It also tested whether the part on accounting for aid is accurate and complete. Readers can see how the yearly oversight cycle for this program is meant to work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-800r:
Currency swings in defense budgeting are reviewed in GAO-05-800R, a letter dated June 16, 2005. The Defense Department spends large sums overseas. It sets exchange rates when it builds its budget. Actual spending then occurs at live rates. If the dollar falls, more dollars are needed than planned. Congress told the department to study other ways to set the rates.

The letter reviews the department's report on that study. The law asked for other approaches to be named. It also asked whether private economic forecasts could be used. And it asked what other agencies do. GAO's review gives Congress a check on whether the study covers what the law required. It frames the choice of method that shapes overseas funding requests.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-860r:
Small business roles in an Alaska gas pipeline are studied in GAO-05-860R, a letter dated August 4, 2005. Alaska holds 35 trillion cubic feet of proven gas. That is about 19 percent of U.S. reserves. A pipeline to the lower 48 states could cost up to $20 billion. A 2004 law told GAO to study small business roles in pipeline building. Congress voiced its view that sponsors should maximize such roles.

GAO found the build is years away at best. Given the approval steps, construction can begin in late 2009 at the earliest. As of June 2005, Alaska had not closed talks with four would-be sponsors. Sponsors must still study in-state gas needs and hold an open season for capacity bids. The letter also notes the sense-of-Congress point is an opinion, not a legal duty. It frames what small firms can expect as the project takes shape.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-890r: A chiropractic benefit for active duty troops is reported in GAO-05-890R, a letter dated September 6, 2005. A 2001 law told the Defense Department to build a plan for the benefit. The department sent Congress its plan in August 2001. The plan covered who qualifies, access, clinic sites, projected costs, and staffing. It also covered marketing and monitoring of the benefit. The hosted text keeps the letter's opening account, so the record shows the benefit was established and how its rollout was framed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-940r:
A public information campaign for digital TV is the topic of GAO-05-940R, a letter dated September 6, 2005. The nation is moving from analog to digital broadcast signals. The shift frees 108 megahertz of spectrum. A 1997 law set 24 megahertz aside for public safety. The rest will be auctioned for wireless services. After the 2001 attacks, freeing the safety spectrum took on new urgency.

The letter takes up issues tied to telling the public about the change. How viewers learn what the switch means for them is its core concern. A clear campaign shapes how smooth the switch will be. The letter gives Congress GAO's account of the campaign questions in one place. It sits beside GAO's other 2005 letters on the transition, which cover subsidy costs and spectrum plans.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-960r:
The federal buying data system gets a progress check in GAO-05-960R, a letter dated September 27, 2005. Government purchases top $300 billion a year. The next-generation system is the only government-wide source on how that money is spent. It was meant to give faster, truer data than the old system. Users were to build their own reports with easier access. A handover period was set to end by October 2005.

GAO tested how far the promised gains have in fact arrived. It read program papers and spoke with the buying agency, the builder, and users. It made many tries at using the system to build reports itself. It also judged whether the system can gather data on interagency deals. The title gives the upshot: improvements are needed. The letter shows where the new system still falls short of its design aims.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-240r:
A fast-track buying power for joint war needs is reviewed in GAO-06-240R, a letter report dated November 22, 2005. Congress worried that urgent joint needs, such as command systems and blue-force tracking, moved too slowly. The fiscal year 2004 defense law gave Joint Forces Command a Limited Acquisition Authority for three years. It lets the command conceive, build, and field answers to surprise joint needs at speed. The law told GAO to measure how much the power was used before it lapses after September 30, 2006.

GAO tracked the command's use of the power in fiscal years 2004 and 2005. It studied the steps and rules the command built to run it. It also named the snags in putting the power to work. GAO did not grade the worth of the gear bought. The letter gives Congress an evidence base for deciding whether the experiment should live on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-30r:
Corrected books at the nuclear regulator are the focus of GAO-06-30R, a letter dated October 27, 2005. Federal agencies must file audited financial statements each year. GAO audits the government's combined statements built from them. During the fiscal 2004 audit, a worrying trend surfaced. More agencies were restating their fiscal 2003 figures to fix errors. Restatements can spring from math slips or misread accounting rules.

This letter covers the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's restatements. It traces the control flaws behind fees owed by licensees that went unrecorded or unbilled. GAO urged the finance chief to test whether new procedures catch every fee. It urged the inspector general to ensure audit steps for such fees are fully applied. Both offices agreed with the advice. The letter belongs to a series on restatements across agencies. Each case teaches the same lesson: small control gaps compound into public doubt.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-40r:
Reserve officers keep a group with a federal charter, and its books were checked. Letter GAO-06-40R, dated October 7, 2005, reviews the audit reports for the Reserve Officers Association. The reports cover the years ended March 31, 2004 and 2003. The group's stated purpose is to back a U.S. military policy that will provide adequate national security for the country.

By law, such chartered groups must present their assets, debts, income, and costs in yearly statements. An outside public accountant must audit those statements. GAO read the statements, the notes, and the reports of the auditor. It found no reportable case of failure to follow the law. The auditor said the statements were presented fairly under U.S. accounting rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-410r:
Military rations meant for hurricane relief were turning up for sale online. A GAO letter report, GAO-06-410R of February 13, 2006, investigates Meals, Ready-To-Eat sold on eBay. Public and congressional interest in the response to Hurricanes Katrina and Rita prompted the work. GAO ran a limited investigation into the claims. The rations were meant for relief efforts after the storms.

GAO focused on selected meals offered for sale. It checked whether they were military issue. Where they were, GAO spoke with sellers to learn how they got them. Readers get a narrow, fact-based inquiry. The letter shows how relief goods can leak into resale markets.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-430r:
How the veterans' health budget is built can decide whether care is funded right. A GAO letter report, GAO-06-430R of February 6, 2006, gives early findings on budget formulation at the Department of Veterans Affairs. The letter records a briefing given to Congress on February 2, 2006. It covers fiscal years 2005 and 2006. It deals with the department's internal process, not later talks with the budget office.

GAO describes how the department builds its budget request for medical programs. It explains the role of the department's actuarial model. It lists activities the department said need more funds. It names factors that drove requests for extra funding. More work was promised later.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-480r:
War plans lean on commercial satellites, and buying that bandwidth had drawn criticism. Letter GAO-06-480R, dated April 17, 2006, sums up Defense Department action on satellite services. The department is the largest single customer of commercial satellite bandwidth. Its use has grown over the past few years. Critics called the buying process lengthy, inflexible, and costly. The department began reexamining how it procures such services.

Congress asked GAO to summarize actions taken so far. Those actions cover revised requirements and a revised buying approach. Readers get a compact status account. The letter does not grade a finished system. It records steps in a reform still under way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-50r:
Cemeteries abroad are paid for in foreign currencies, so exchange rates shape their budgets. Letter GAO-06-50R, dated October 20, 2005, reviews the American Battle Monuments Commission's currency account. The account guards the spending power of funds when the dollar falls. A fiscal year 2005 appropriations report required the review. Conferees worried the budget office had not handled rate effects well for fiscal year 2005.

GAO examined the commission's old method for forecasting exchange rates. It tracked changes in the fund as the dollar depreciated. It also reviewed changes made for the fiscal year 2006 budget filing. The title notes a new approach to forecasting rates.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-510r:
The Boy Scouts keep a charter from Congress, and the audit of their books is reviewed here. Letter GAO-06-510R, dated March 14, 2006, covers the Boy Scouts of America. The audit reports run for fiscal year 2003. The group's purpose is to teach boys to do things for themselves and for others. It trains them in scoutcraft and teaches them values such as courage and self-reliance, along with love of country.

By law, such chartered groups must present their assets, debts, income, and costs in yearly statements. An outside public accountant must audit those statements. GAO read the statements and the reports of the auditor. Its review found no reportable case of failure to follow the law. The auditor said the statements were presented fairly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-680r:
Children caught in the Gulf Coast hurricanes are the focus of GAO-06-680R, a briefing document dated May 11, 2006. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita displaced huge numbers of families in 2005. Children faced lost schooling, separation from parents, and risks to their safety. GAO gathered lessons on how agencies protected children and got them back into class. The work drew on federal and nonprofit groups active in the response.

GAO shared the briefing with officials from the Departments of Health and Human Services and Education. Officials from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children also reviewed it. They generally agreed with the conclusions or gave technical fixes that GAO folded in. GAO made no recommendations at this time. The briefing preserves early lessons for the next mass displacement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-690r:
Medical training is the cause behind the group whose audit GAO reviewed in GAO-06-690R, a letter dated May 12, 2006. The National Fund for Medical Education holds a federal charter. It seeks to improve how doctors and other medical staff are trained. Chartered groups must file yearly financial statements and have them audited by an independent public accountant. The statements lay out what the group owns and owes, and what it took in and spent.

For this fund, the audit covered the fiscal year ended December 31, 2003. GAO read the auditor's reports and found no reportable breaches of the law's reporting rules. In the auditor's opinion, the statements were fairly presented under United States generally accepted accounting principles. GAO's letter sends that result to Congress, which keeps watch over federal charters like this one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-70r:
A restated federal balance sheet is explained in GAO-06-70R, a GAO financial audit letter dated December 6, 2005. GAO audits the consolidated financial statements of the United States government each year. During that work, GAO scrutinized the General Services Administration's fiscal year 2003 statements. The agency manages federal buildings and other shared services. A problem in its building accounts forced a formal restatement.

GAO found that costs for one major construction project were wrongly moved between accounts. The costs left the Construction in Process account and entered the Buildings account. That improper transfer caused a material misstatement in two line items of the 2003 balance sheet. The letter records why the restatement was needed and what it corrected.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-820r:
Commuter rail contracts are inventoried in GAO-06-820R, a letter report GAO issued on July 10, 2006. Commuter rail carried more than 420 million passenger trips in 2005. Several of the largest agencies hire their own staff to run trains. Many others contract out the work to Amtrak, freight railroads, or private operators. Those contracts cover services that are critical to daily operations. The letter was sent to the Senate banking committee chairman.

The letter lists the active service contracts of commuter rail agencies. It identifies which agencies rely on outside operators and which firms hold the work. Such an inventory shows how much of a public service rests on private hands. It also gives lawmakers a base for questions on cost and accountability. GAO presents the data without a broader audit judgment.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-130r:
Federal unemployment taxes flow into a trust fund that pays jobless benefits. This GAO letter, GAO-07-130R, dated November 3, 2006, reports a set of agreed-upon procedures on those flows. The Labor Department agreed to the procedures and concurred in their use. The work covers the fiscal year ended September 30, 2006. Its aim was narrow: check whether the net tax revenue sent to the Unemployment Trust Fund matched the records.

The procedures tested the transactions behind the amounts distributed. They also covered key reconciliations between tax agency records and Treasury records. GAO performed the work under government auditing standards. The letter stresses that the procedures were only those the department agreed to. An enclosure lists each procedure and GAO's findings from carrying it out. Readers who need assurance beyond those checks must judge the procedures' adequacy themselves.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-240r:
The Army is destroying a nerve agent stockpile in Indiana, and the waste plan drew scrutiny. GAO reviewed the cost study behind that plan in GAO-07-240R, dated January 26, 2007. The Newport depot held 1,269 tons of VX nerve agent. A water and caustic mix breaks the agent down. The process yields about 2 million gallons of liquid waste. By December 1, 2006, about 34 percent of the stockpile was neutralized. None of the waste had yet been treated.

Cutting five of eight treatment options looked reasonable, GAO found. The cost figures behind the choice did not. GAO found many errors and gaps in the estimates. No outside check of the math had been done. That made the savings of the favored DuPont plan uncertain. The Army's plan ships the waste off-site for treatment. GAO gave four steps to rebuild trust in the numbers. The Defense Department agreed with them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-260r:
Childhood obesity keeps climbing, and experts rank more movement as the top fix. GAO surveyed what shapes children's activity in GAO-07-260R, dated December 6, 2006. Obesity among children ages 6 to 11 rose from 15.1 percent in 1999 to 18.8 percent in 2004. The health department projects 20 percent of youth obese by 2010. Obese children cost the health system about three times the average. Congress asked what drives activity levels down.

GAO reviewed research articles rather than running new studies. The factors fell into three groups. The first covers traits like family income and race. The second covers attitudes, beliefs, and screen habits. The third covers neighborhoods and school activity options. No single factor explains the trend, the review says. Studies call for better measures of activity and sitting time. The letter points readers to the full set of cited work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-30r:
Most of the Pentagon's Iraq rebuilding money was committed by late 2006, but much work remained. GAO took stock in GAO-07-30R, a letter dated December 15, 2006. In fiscal year 2004, Congress provided $18.4 billion for Iraq relief and rebuilding. The defense department received the largest share of that money. GAO tracked progress on the building work. It also tracked the support costs that contractors charged.

About 29 percent of the building program was unfinished, GAO found. The rest of the work was due by mid- to late 2008. Support costs for the design-build deals ran high. They reached about 33 percent of the contract value. Security alone consumed a large share, some $359.6 million in all. The department has begun hiring Iraqi firms directly. That shift may cut costs and add local jobs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-410r: The VA was sitting on mystery money in 2007 — GAO's letter says late and shaky data on unspent balances hobbled smart decisions. The findings demand timely, honest books from the department. The letter's point is basic: you cannot spend wisely what you cannot see clearly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-470r: The blinded veterans' finances got checked in 2007, and GAO's letter audits the association's financial statements in full detail. The findings give the formal opinion for the record. The letter proves the auditor's reach honors no exemption, however deserved. The blinded vets deserved both honor and honesty.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-510r: The nation's long-term fiscal outlook was grim in January 2007, and GAO's letter updates the red-ink forecast for Congress. The findings recycle the stark math. The letter's message does not soften: the debt was not waiting for anyone. The numbers did not negotiate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-540r: Training new border agents was a 2007 priority — GAO's letter briefs Congress on how the rookies were being prepared for duty. The findings size up the training pipeline. The letter's theme: the border is only as strong as its newest guardians.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-610r: Rail safety got its follow-up grilling in 2007, and GAO's letter answers Congress's post-hearing questions on the railroad watch. The findings fill the gaps the testimony left. The letter keeps the safety debate supplied with facts instead of slogans.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-640r: The defense-services buying spree got its Q&A in 2007 — GAO's letter answers the record's questions on the acquisition binge. The findings fill in the gaps for Congress in detail. The letter feeds the debate over the Pentagon's service-contract habit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-670r: Little League's books got the federal once-over in 2007 — GAO's letter audits the youth baseball group's finances for the year. The findings deliver the formal opinion. The letter shows the chartered-corporation watch stretches from Congress all the way to the ballfield.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-790r: Old soldiers' healthcare needed a closer watch in 2007 — GAO's letter says oversight of the Armed Forces Retirement Home's medical care should toughen. The findings target the care behind the gates. The letter's duty: those who served deserve watched-over care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-10r: GAO wrote Congress in 2007 on the Pentagon's training lands — the ranges where troops learn to fight. The reports on keeping those lands fit for use were getting better, GAO said, but the grading of each range and the master plan still needed work. The letter tracks slow gains in guarding the ground the military trains on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-190r: GAO wrote Congress in 2007 with a map of the energy agency's oil and gas research bets. The letter lists what Washington was funding to push drill tech and cleaner ways to pull fuel from the ground. With pump prices high and energy a hot topic, the report shows where public research dollars were aimed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-270r: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on status of Selected Aspects of the Coast Guard's Deepwater Program. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-330r: This 2007 GAO report takes a hard look at telecommunications: Preliminary Information on Media Ownership. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-370r: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on military Personnel: Guidance Needed for Any Future Conversions of Military Medical Positions to Civilian Positions. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-580r: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on DOD Personnel Clearances: Questions for the Record Related to the Quality and Timeliness of Clearances. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-790r: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at military Personnel: DOD Needs Data to Determine if Active Duty Service Has an Impact on the Ability of Guard and Reservists to Maintain Their Civilian Professio. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-800r: The Government Accountability Office dug into refund Anticipation Loans in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-830r: GAO published its findings on defense Management: Assessment of the Reorganization of the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
